title: Making Decisions That Negatively Impact People You Care About
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article addresses one of leadership's most painful obligations: making calls that harm people the leader genuinely cares about, for the sake of the larger organization. The author lays out a three-step approach for handling the aftermath: acknowledge the difficulty and pain of the decision honestly, walk people through the reasoning and process behind it rather than merely justifying the outcome, and proactively offer concrete support to those affected. A key distinction closes the piece, between remorse (feeling bad about the impact) and regret (wishing you'd chosen differently). The author argues good leaders should feel remorseful but not regretful, since a decision made with the same facts and same care would be the right one again, even if it's painful.
points: Leaders must prioritize the organization's health over any individual's needs, even people they care about
A three-step response helps leaders navigate the aftermath: acknowledge, explain, and support
Good leaders explain the reasoning behind a hard call rather than simply justifying it
Remorse over a decision's impact is appropriate; regret over the decision itself is not, if it was the right call
quotes: Perhaps the hardest task in leadership is making decisions that negatively impact people the leader cares about.
Leaders must always hold the health and survival of the organization and team above the needs of any individual, no matter how much they care about them.
Second, they offer the details behind the decision, explaining the painstaking steps used in reaching the conclusion.
Third, they provide the support those impacted need to navigate the changes and consequences of the decision.
This means good leaders don’t regret the decision even if they feel remorseful about it.
